awd_titl_txt: CAREER: The Role of Ice-Nucleating Particles and Their Feedback on Clouds in Warming Arctic Climate
awd_abstract_narration:
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

The Arctic is warming rapidly – faster than the rest of the world. A number of processes have been proposed for this so-called Arctic polar amplification. While sea ice is known to play an important role on reflecting solar radiation and altering the Earth’s surface temperature, the roles of other processes are difficult to quantify. Especially, contributions from atmospheric mechanisms associated with ice-nucleating particles (INP; a few in a million aerosol particles below -20 °C) and ice-involved clouds remain uncertain in the Arctic. This project aims to fill the gap by investigating the sources (natural/manmade), atmospheric abundance/budget, chemical composition and physical properties of INPs in the Atlantic sector of the Arctic. Moreover, the large measurement uncertainties in number concentrations, chemical composition and sources of INPs are problematic for modeling real-life phenomena. This research targets minimizing the measurement uncertainties and addresses this critical deficiency through a series of studies that involve direct collection of ice-nucleating particles and their residuals. To characterize Arctic ice-nucleating particles, a novel portable ice nucleation experiment chamber and a cold stage-supported droplet freezing assay will be used to obtain freezing temperature spectra of airborne particle samples. A new inertial ice particle separation technique will be used to collect ice crystal residuals relevant to the Arctic ice-involved clouds. The subsequent offline microspectroscopic characterization of ice crystal residuals and ambient aerosol particles will reveal the relative importance of aerosol physicochemical properties to particle size in ice nucleation. Ultimately, the measurements of INPs and ice crystal residuals from this research will be parameterized and translated to describe the time-resolved freezing ability of the particles as a function of temperature, their composition, water activity parameters and other physicochemical properties. Finally, an integration of research and education is the most important target of this project. This project will involve two graduate and several undergraduate students in research, curriculum development and outreach, as these are learning experiences that can aid in their professional development. This project will also develop hands-on curricular modules integrated with the proposed research to teach environmental and climate science to the general public, promote college courses and train future scientists.

Currently, there is a critical deficiency in Arctic field data regarding the abundance and composition of atmospheric ice-nucleating particles at temperatures above -15 °C. This project will fill this gap by experimentally elucidating abundance and physicochemical properties of ice-nucleating particles. State-of-the-art representations of high-temperature INPs from the Atlantic sector of the Arctic will advance the atmospheric modeling community’s knowledge of the ice nucleation processes and its formulation in the Earth’s energy balance. The project also aims to provide robust and well-characterized INP measurements that will be archived in the publicly available university database. The measurements from this project, in collaboration with the existing transnational Arctic research community, will improve the understanding of the nature of aerosols, and the INP parameterizations representative of the Ny-Ålesund site will dramatically improve the understanding of ice formation processes that are currently very poorly represented in climate models. In addition, this research activity directly aligns with one of the NSF’s 10 priority research areas, “Navigating the New Arctic”.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, yet key processes driving this rapid change remain poorly understood. One important process involves rare ice-nucleating particles (INPs), which trigger ice formation in arctic clouds and influence cloud lifetime, precipitation, and the amount of sunlight reflected to space. These cloud processes play a critical role in regulating the arctic system. The goal of this project was to understand how INPs affect arctic clouds and contribute by integrating field observations, laboratory experiments, and atmospheric modeling simulations.

This project addressed a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science: identifying which natural particles initiate ice formation in arctic clouds, where they originate, and how they vary across seasons. To answer these questions, Hiranuma and his team established long-term collaborations with European scientists and analyzed aerosol samples collected in Ny-Alesund, Svalbard, a high-arctic research settlement. The team also deployed specialized instruments capable of autonomously measuring rare INP abundance in the atmosphere (often a few or less in a million particles). By integrating field observations with laboratory analyses, the project improved understanding of the physical, chemical, and biological properties of particles that drive arctic cloud ice formation.

Over the award period (2020-2026), the project demonstrated that arctic INPs vary seasonally and are influenced by both marine biological activity and long-range continental transport. Laboratory analyses revealed differences in particle composition, including mineral dust, biogenic material, and organic compounds, providing new insight into why some particles are much more effective at initiating ice formation than others. The project also generated new measurements needed to improve ice nucleation parameterizations used in numerical weather prediction and atmospheric models. These results contribute to reducing uncertainties in simulations of arctic clouds and their influence on Earth system change.

The project also produced important technological advances. Researchers designed, tested, and validated improved sampling systems capable of separating cloud ice particles from surrounding aerosols, enabling more accurate laboratory characterization than previously possible. Complementary laboratory methods, including droplet freezing experiments and microscopic chemical analyses, provided a comprehensive understanding of the particles responsible for cloud ice formation. These measurement capabilities strengthen future atmospheric research and provide valuable tools for the broader scientific community studying aerosols, clouds, and precipitation.

Education and workforce development were central components of the project. 14 funded research trainees, including 9 undergraduate students, 4 graduate thesis students, one postdoctoral researcher, and several international collaborators, received hands-on training in atmospheric measurements, laboratory instrumentation, computational data analysis, and scientific communication through this interdisciplinary project. Students participated in 5 peer-reviewed research publications (several more underway), >20 conference presentations, and collaborative projects with national and international partners. Many trainees gained valuable experience working across disciplines including atmospheric science, chemistry, environmental science, engineering, and physics, strengthening the next generation of atmospheric scientists and researchers.

The project also transformed classroom education by integrating real-world research data into university courses. New instructional materials were developed to teach scientific programming, numerical analysis, and environmental data analysis using real arctic observations. Python-based educational modules were created in both English and Spanish, increasing accessibility for students in the West Texas community and providing educational resources that can continue to benefit future students beyond the lifetime of the award.

The project's educational impact extended beyond the university through hands-on outreach activities on cloud formation, arctic system change, and atmospheric chemistry. More than 3,000 K-12 students, many from rural communities, participated in these programs. The project also developed lending kits, bilingual educational resources, standards-aligned teacher materials, and freely accessible instructional content to support long-term classroom use. Collaborations with schools, museums, nonprofit organizations, and the Polar STEAM program further expanded the reach and sustainability of these educational efforts.

International collaboration was another defining feature of the project. A dozen renowned scientists from 15 partner organizations in the United States, Italy, and Germany worked together to collect samples, perform laboratory analyses, and interpret observations. Despite travel restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic, the team successfully maintained research momentum through remote experiments, virtual laboratory campaigns, and coordinated international sampling efforts. These collaborations demonstrated the resilience of modern scientific partnerships while providing students with valuable experience working in global research teams, creating lasting partnerships that will support future arctic and atmospheric science in our nation.

Overall, this NSF CAREER project yielded new insights regarding the role of INPs in arctic clouds while integrating research, education, and outreach. It generated new knowledge to improve weather and Earth system models, trained a diverse STEM workforce, incorporated cutting-edge research into university classrooms, and inspired thousands of K-12 students through hands-on atmospheric science activities. These lasting contributions strengthen both scientific understanding of arctic system change and the preparation of future scientists to address complex environmental challenges.
